summary: Gives network operators advice on deploying 6to4, an automatic technique for tunneling IPv6 over IPv4. It is aimed at ISPs, including those that do not yet support IPv6, and at content providers, with some advice for implementers. The goal is fewer unhappy users and help-desk calls.

eli5.summary: 6to4 lets IPv6 traffic sneak through old IPv4 roads. This is a guide for the road crews on how to run it so fewer people get stuck or call to complain.

subtitle: How to deploy and manage 6to4 IPv6-over-IPv4 tunneling without causing support problems

tldr.problem: 6to4 is an automatic way for IPv6 traffic to travel over IPv4 networks when ISPs do not yet support IPv6. However, it has been deployed widely (often unintentionally by end users) and causes mysterious connection failures about 10 to 20 percent of the time, making help desks blame IPv6 instead of the method.
tldr.mechanism: This document advises ISPs, content providers, and implementers on how to configure and operate 6to4 relays, filter protocol 41 packets correctly, manage routing, and diagnose problems so users get fewer timeouts and help desk calls.
tldr.outcome: Well-configured 6to4 infrastructure reduces user frustration and improves the chances that IPv6 adoption will proceed smoothly rather than being dismissed as unreliable.

today: RFC 6343 is Informational, published in August 2011. A companion document, RFC 6891, subsequently proposed to reclassify 6to4 as Historic due to widespread deployment problems and the availability of better alternatives. However, millions of hosts and CPE routers still implement 6to4, so the operational guidance in RFC 6343 remains relevant for operators managing networks where 6to4 users exist.

sections.title: What 6to4 Is and Why It Matters
sections.content:
6to4 is an automatic tunneling technique defined in RFC 3056 and RFC 3068 that lets a computer with a global IPv4 address automatically create an IPv6 address and route IPv6 packets through an IPv4-only network. The computer encapsulates IPv6 packets inside IPv4 (using IP protocol 41) and sends them to a relay router that decapsulates them and forwards them into native IPv6. This was intended to encourage early IPv6 adoption when native IPv6 connectivity was scarce.

However, 6to4 is widely deployed unintentionally: many router vendors ship it enabled by default, and many desktop operating systems enable it by default. Measurements show it fails 9 to 20 percent of the time due to firewalls dropping protocol 41 packets, misconfigured relays, and other operational problems. When a user sees a slow connection that eventually falls back to IPv4, they often do not realize 6to4 is involved, and help desks simply advise disabling IPv6, defeating the purpose of the technology.
sections.eli5: 6to4 is like a tunnel through an old IPv4 highway so IPv6 traffic can get through. It should work automatically, but routers and firewalls sometimes block it silently, causing mysterious hangs before falling back to the old way. This tells operators how to run relays and pass traffic so users do not get stuck.

sections.title: How 6to4 Works
sections.content:
A 6to4-enabled site or host with IPv4 address V4ADDR automatically claims the IPv6 prefix 2002:V4ADDR::/48. For example, a router at 192.0.2.170 becomes 2002:c000:2aa::/48. A 6to4 relay is a router that has both IPv4 and native IPv6 connectivity. It announces a route to 2002::/16 in IPv6, telling the world that it will decapsulate IPv6-over-IPv4 packets bound for 2002::/16 addresses. In the anycast variant, all relays listen on the same IPv4 address (192.88.99.1), and routing directs packets to the nearest relay.

When a 6to4 host sends an IPv6 packet to a native IPv6 destination, it encapsulates it in IPv4 and sends it to 192.88.99.1. An anycast relay receives it, decapsulates it, and forwards it into native IPv6. The return packet arrives at a relay (possibly a different one) that encapsulates it back and sends it to the original 6to4 host. This is seamless if relays are present and configured correctly.
sections.eli5: A 6to4 host turns its IPv4 address into a fake IPv6 address, wraps IPv6 packets inside IPv4 envelopes, and mails them to 192.88.99.1, where a relay opens them and forwards the IPv6 packets for real. Return packets come back the same way.

sections.title: Why 6to4 Fails in Practice
sections.content:
Empirical studies show 6to4 failures fall into several categories. Outbound black hole: Packets to 192.88.99.1 are silently dropped by a firewall or misconfigured relay instead of being relayed. Inbound black hole: Relay response packets using IP protocol 41 are dropped by a stateful firewall at the user's site unless they come from 192.88.99.1. No return relay: The return path reaches an unwilling relay that rejects packets, or no relay announces a route to 2002::/16 at all.

Path MTU failures: The maximum packet size over a 6to4 tunnel is smaller than 1500 bytes due to encapsulation, but servers default to 1500. Path MTU Discovery does not always work, causing full-size TCP packets to be dropped silently. Reverse DNS failure: 6to4-addressed hosts rarely have reverse DNS, which can be mistaken for spoofing. Bogus addresses: Sites using private or undocumented IPv4 addresses cannot reach the Internet even if 6to4 activates. Rogue router advertisements: Misconfigured devices issue IPv6 router advertisements on the wrong interfaces, advertising 2002::/16 and confusing IPv6 hosts.
sections.eli5: 6to4 breaks in many ways: relays disappear, firewalls block the tunnel, packet sizes get too big and get dropped silently, and misconfigured routers send bad directions. Each failure mode causes mysterious timeouts.

sections.title: What Operators and Vendors Should Do
sections.content:
Vendors: Never enable 6to4 by default in routers or operating systems. Any implementation that activates 6to4 when the IPv4 address is in RFC 1918 private space is buggy and must be fixed. Relays must follow RFC 4213 carefully to handle MTU issues correctly.

ISPs without IPv6: Check whether 192.88.99.1 is reachable, functional, and willing to relay your traffic. If not, block it and send an ICMP 'destination unreachable' message so 6to4 fails fast instead of hanging. Allow protocol 41 packets; do not silently drop them. Do not use 'bogon' IPv4 addresses (like 1.1.1.0/24) for customers. If you run Carrier Grade NAT, be aware that 6to4 will not work correctly.

ISPs with IPv6: Advise users to disable 6to4 and use native IPv6 instead. Run a well-managed 6to4 relay of your own or peer with one. Do not leave 6to4 relays enabled by default on routers. Defend against rogue router advertisements.

Transit ISPs and content providers: Operate a 6to4 relay, carefully announce 192.88.99.0/24 and 2002::/16, allow protocol 41, allow ICMPv6, ensure sufficient performance and MTU handling, and set the relay's IPv4 source address to 192.88.99.1 for return packets to avoid stateful firewall problems.
sections.eli5: Vendors should stop shipping 6to4 enabled. ISPs without IPv6 should either offer a relay or block it clearly. ISPs with IPv6 should tell users to use real IPv6. Big operators should run their own relays if needed.

sections.title: Relay Configuration and Performance
sections.content:
A 6to4 relay is stateless: it simply encapsulates or decapsulates packets. Multiple relays can load-share traffic to the same anycast address. Relays must respond to ICMPv6 echo requests, enforce rate limits high enough that ICMP errors are not dropped (1000 packets per second or more on a busy relay), allow IPv6 PMTUD (Path MTU Discovery), and use IPv4 source address 192.88.99.1 when replying to 6to4 clients to avoid stateful firewall rejections. The relay must announce 2002::/16 in IPv6 routing with appropriate scope: too narrow and users cannot reach it, too broad and non-customers get free service.

Content servers should set their IPv6 MTU to 1280 bytes (the IPv6 minimum) to avoid PMTUD failures. They should not rely on reverse DNS for security checks and should not advertise 6to4 addresses in DNS AAAA records—if they have IPv6, it should be native. Managed tunnels such as tunnel brokers, 6rd, and L2TPv2 are better alternatives for carriers that want to offer tunneled IPv6 to customers.
sections.eli5: A relay is simple: it just wraps and unwraps packets. The tricky parts are running it fast enough, letting error messages through, not blocking ICMPv6, and using the right source address so firewalls do not drop replies.
